standard.title: Authors’ use of punctuation
standard.description: understand how authors use and experiment with punctuation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing sources formally and informally (AC9E9LA09). They have not yet analysed how authors use and experiment with punctuation for stylistic and rhetorical effects.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how authors use and experiment with punctuation.

nodes.label: Punctuation for detail and extension
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how authors use specific punctuation (colons, semicolons, ellipses) to add detail, extend ideas or create particular effects in texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one use of a specific punctuation mark (colon, semicolon or ellipsis) in a provided text and explain the effect it creates.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain the use of colons, semicolons and ellipses across expository and literary texts, explaining how each punctuation choice creates a different effect.
wider: Compare how the same punctuation mark (e.g. the colon) creates different effects in academic versus literary versus dialogue contexts
Examine how authors use colons and semicolons differently from the standard rules to create expressive effects in literary prose
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use punctuation experimentally to represent oral speech patterns or cultural storytelling rhythms in print
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to understand experimental and unconventional punctuation — a move that depends on understanding conventional use first. Students who cannot identify standard punctuation effects cannot recognise or evaluate deliberate departures from those conventions.

response_modes.reason: Recognition and explanation of specific punctuation marks (colon, semicolon, ellipsis) and their effects requires practice across examples — students need familiarity with conventional use before they can meaningfully analyse experimentation.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific punctuation mark and names the effect it creates
Explains how the punctuation choice contributes to meaning or style in the text

nodes.label: Punctuation for emotion, tentativeness and experiment
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can understand how authors experiment with punctuation to represent emotions, create tentativeness or achieve stylistic effects, including unconventional uses.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of experimental or expressive punctuation use in a text and explain the effect the author intended.
nodes.typical_width: Examine how authors use ellipses for tentativeness, multiple exclamation marks for emotion, and other unconventional punctuation for effect, across a range of literary and digital texts.
wider: Compare how digital communication contexts (social media, messaging) have expanded the expressive use of punctuation emojis and unconventional marks, and evaluate whether these are ‘experimental’ in the same sense as literary punctuation
Examine how Modernist authors (e.g. Virginia Woolf, Samuel Beckett) used unconventional punctuation as part of their literary style — compare to contemporary experimental writers
Analyse how punctuation experimentation in poetry (e.g. Emily Dickinson’s dashes) creates unique rhythm and meaning

response_modes.reason: Experimental punctuation looks very different in literary prose, poetry and digital communication — students who only encounter one context may think experimentation means informality rather than deliberate craft; contrasting contexts resolve this.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of experimental punctuation across literary history and digital communication is substantial and offers rich comparative work — from Dickinson’s dashes to digital emoji punctuation, the context variation is genuinely enriching.
success_criteria: Identifies an example of experimental or expressive punctuation in a text
Explains the intended effect of the unconventional punctuation choice
